analysis.one_liner: Banned health plans from placing stricter limits and higher cost-sharing on mental health and addiction care than on physical care.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 203 cosponsors — 173 House Democrats, 29 Republicans, and the House's sole Independent — but was referred to three committees and never received a single vote in the 107th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required health plans to treat mental health and substance abuse coverage the same as coverage for physical illness. Plans could not charge higher copays, impose lower visit limits, or set lower annual and lifetime caps on mental health or addiction treatment than they do on medical and surgical care. It would have closed loopholes in the existing 1996 parity law — the exemption that let employers opt out by claiming a cost increase, and the law's expiration date — and it would have extended the rules to people buying insurance on their own. It never came up for a vote in any committee or on the House floor.
analysis.who_benefits: People with mental illness and substance use disorders — and their families — gain the most, because the bill would have forced insurance plans to cover mental health and addiction care on the same financial terms as physical care: same copays, same visit limits, same annual and lifetime caps [S2] [S3]. Workers and families with employer coverage were the main audience, since most group plans are governed by the ERISA provisions the bill amended, but it also covered people buying individual insurance [S3]. Employers and insurers who already offered equal benefits would face a level playing field rather than being undercut by rivals with skimpier mental health coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with mental illness or addiction

how_it_helps.text: It barred group and individual health plans from imposing treatment limits or higher cost-sharing on mental health benefits unless the same limits apply to medical and surgical benefits, so people with depression, anxiety, or addiction would pay the same copays and get the same visit counts as someone treated for a physical illness [S2].
It extended the same parity rules to substance abuse and chemical dependency benefits, a category often singled out for the strictest caps [S2].

It closed two loopholes in the existing 1996 federal parity law: the exemption letting employers claim a cost increase to opt out, and the law's automatic expiration (sunset) date, making the requirement permanent [S3].
It applied to individual health insurance coverage as well as employer group plans, protecting people who buy coverage on their own [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers would bear the cost of richer mental health and addiction benefits, since plans could no longer use low visit caps, higher copays, or lower annual and lifetime limits to hold down spending on those conditions [S2] [S3]. Some of that cost would likely be passed to policyholders through premiums; the existing law's exemption for small employers claiming a cost increase would have been eliminated [S3].

drawbacks.text: Parity requirements can raise premiums, since plans that can no longer limit mental health visits or charge higher copays for them face higher claims costs; the bill removed even the existing law's exemption for small employers and its expiration date, extending that cost to all covered plans [S2] [S3].

The bill did not require any plan to cover mental health or substance abuse treatment at all — it only barred unequal limits for plans that choose to offer those benefits — so a plan could have avoided the requirement by dropping the coverage entirely [S3].

Insurers retained broad authority to manage mental health benefits through prior authorization, pre-admission screening, and medical-necessity rules, so the parity guarantee depended on how plans applied those tools [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit was real: it would have ended a common practice of charging people with mental illness and addiction higher copays, lower visit caps, and lower annual and lifetime limits than people with physical illness pay, and it applied to individual insurance as well as employer plans [S2] [S3]. The main cost, as opponents argued at the time, would have been higher premiums, since insurers could no longer hold down costs by skimping on mental health coverage; some plans might also have dropped mental health benefits altogether, since the bill requires parity only for plans that already offer them and does not mandate the benefit itself [S2] [S3]. The bill left insurers room to manage care through prior authorization and medical-necessity screening, which limited the guarantee in practice [S3]. On balance it was a consumer-protection measure whose costs fell on insurance plans and employers rather than on patients directly, and the record — 203 cosponsors and no committee vote — shows the cost argument won without a public test.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced, got handed down to two subcommittees in February and March 2001, and then sat with no action, no committee vote, and no floor vote for the rest of the two-year Congress.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on January 3, 2001 and referred the same day to the Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees [S5].

In February and March 2001 it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee and the Education and the Workforce Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee; the action record shows no markup, committee vote, or floor action after that [S5].

Despite support from 203 House members across both parties — 173 Democrats, 29 Republicans, and the House's one Independent — the bill never came to any vote before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S4] [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers that would have borne the cost of equalized mental health and addiction coverage kept the status quo, since the bill never reached a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers; the parity rules never arrived

for.name: Rep. Marge Roukema
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 3, 2001, amending ERISA, the Public Health Service Act, and the tax code to require parity for mental health and substance abuse benefits [S1] [S3].

for.name: 173 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making up the large majority of its 203 cosponsors [S4].

for.name: 29 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support in both parties [S4].

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders (I-VT)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; he was also one of the 28 original co-introducers listed at introduction [S3] [S4].

against.name: Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair Billy Tauzin, R-LA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced, referred it to the Health Subcommittee on February 7, 2001, and never reported it out for a House vote [S5].

against.name: Education and the Workforce Committee (Chair John Boehner, R-OH)
against.role: Sharing jurisdiction over employer health plans under ERISA
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and referred it to the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee on March 2, 2001; no further action was ever recorded [S5].

against.name: Ways and Means Committee (Chair Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.role: Sharing jurisdiction over the tax-code provisions governing employer plans
against.what_they_did: Received the bill but the action record shows no subcommittee referral, markup, or vote on it [S5].

against.name: Health insurers and employer coalitions
against.role: Industry groups opposing the parity mandate
against.what_they_did: Opposed full mental health parity legislation during this period on grounds of premium and administrative costs, pressing Congress to keep the weaker 1996 parity law.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: 173 of 208 House Democrats, 29 of 223 House Republicans, and the chamber's sole Independent cosponsored, but the committees that buried the bill were all chaired by Republicans who did not act on it.

industries.note: Insurers would lose the ability to impose stricter visit limits, copays, and annual or lifetime caps on mental health and addiction care than on physical care, and could no longer use the small-employer cost exemption or rely on an expiration date. Their cost of doing business rises; whether premiums rise for customers is the industry's standing argument against parity.

industries.industry: Employers offering health benefits (including self-insured plans under ERISA)
industries.note: The bill amended ERISA and the tax code directly, so employer-sponsored plans would bear the cost of equalized benefits, which is why employer groups fought parity mandates. For employees, the same rule means better coverage for conditions that are common and treatable.

industries.industry: Mental health and substance abuse treatment providers
industries.note: Therapists, psychiatric hospitals, and addiction treatment programs would see demand for their services better covered, since patients would no longer hit artificially low visit caps or unaffordable cost-sharing for mental health and addiction care.
